nameStory: The name 'atomus' comes from the Latin word for 'atom,' referring to this snail's incredibly tiny size - it's one of the smallest marine snails in the world! These microscopic mollusks are so small they were only discovered with the help of magnifying equipment, living up to their atomic-sized reputation.
description: Omalogyra atomus is an absolutely tiny marine snail that's almost impossible to see without a magnifying glass or microscope. These microscopic mollusks measure less than 1 millimeter across - about the size of a grain of fine sand! The shell is nearly transparent, colorless to pale white, and coiled in a flat spiral like a miniature nautilus. Despite their size, they're true snails with all the typical snail features, just scaled down to an almost invisible level.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Less than 1mm across - smaller than most grains of sand and nearly invisible to the naked eye, requiring magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Flat spiral shell
idTips.description: Shell coiled in a tight, flat spiral like a tiny disk or miniature nautilus, with about 3-4 whorls visible under magnification

idTips.label: Transparent appearance
idTips.description: Shell is nearly colorless and translucent, appearing like a tiny glass bead when viewed under magnification

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: Shell surface appears completely smooth and glossy under magnification, lacking any ridges or obvious sculptural details

idTips.label: Marine habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in saltwater environments, often among seaweed and marine debris in tidal areas

habitat: These microscopic snails live in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and among seaweed beds. They're often found clinging to algae, kelp, or hiding in the sediment and organic matter that collects in protected rocky crevices. Look for them in the intertidal zone where they can survive both underwater and brief exposure during low tide.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm, though their tiny size makes observation challenging year-round. Best found by examining seaweed and algae under magnification.
seasonality.summer: Most active during warmer months when they feed and reproduce. Can be found on various types of marine algae in tide pools and shallow waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be harder to locate as some seaweed dies back. Continue searching among persistent algae and in sediment.
seasonality.winter: Less active in colder waters but still present. May be deeper in sediment or more protected areas during harsh weather.

funFact: Despite being smaller than most grains of sand, Omalogyra atomus can actually swim by flapping its tiny foot like a fin - making it one of the few snails capable of true swimming rather than just crawling!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other microscopic marine organisms or even mistaken for tiny particles of sand or debris. The key difference is the distinct spiral shell structure visible under magnification - most other microscopic marine life lacks this characteristic coiled shell pattern.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the most extreme examples of miniaturization in the mollusk world, showing how evolution can pack all the complexity of a snail into an almost impossibly small package. Their discovery and study has been greatly aided by modern microscopy techniques.
compareHints: As the only Omalogyra species reliably recorded in New England waters, it's most easily compared to other tiny marine snails in the region. Unlike rissooid snails which have more elongated, tower-like shells, Omalogyra atomus has its characteristic flat, disk-like spiral. Other microscopic marine snails typically have more pronounced shell sculpture or different proportions even at tiny sizes.
